h1: The 5 Best Jackery Portable Power Stations of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Jackery Power Stations: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 5 Jackery portable power stations scored on capacity, charging speed, expandability and home backup use.
summary: The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is the one most households should buy, with 1070Wh, 1500W output and one-hour fast charging. The Explorer 2000 v2 is the choice for people who want 2 kWh in the smallest body, while the Explorer 2000 Plus adds expansion up to 24 kWh. The HomePower 3600 Plus is the home-backup option, and the Explorer 300 is the light weekend unit.
intro: A power station is two numbers wearing one label: how much energy it stores, in watt-hours, and how much it can deliver at once, in watts. People buy on the first and get burned by the second. A 1070Wh battery can run a laptop for days, but a 1500W kettle will drain it in about half an hour, and anything above its watt rating will not run at all.

We ranked five Jackery stations, from a $200 to $500 compact to $500-plus large models, by reviewing their listings for capacity, output, charging speed, expansion and intended use. Jackery sells similar names across several generations, so we gave extra weight to stated figures such as 1070Wh and 66-minute charging over slogans like built to last.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 Portable Power Station, 1070Wh, 1500W
products.verdict: 1070Wh and 1500W with one-hour fast charging and a 10 year lifespan, at a mid-range price.
products.description:
The Explorer 1000 v2 stores 1070Wh, outputs 1500W, charges fast in about one hour and lists a 10 year lifespan. The 1500W output covers a coffee maker, a microwave or a small space heater for short stretches, which is the dividing line between a camping battery and a household tool.

It takes first place because it is the only Jackery here at the $200 to $500 bracket that combines that wattage with a stated charge time. The Explorer 300 is cheaper and lighter but holds far less, and the 2000 models cost more for capacity most buyers do not need.

Buy it for car camping, outages and van life. Its 1070Wh does not run a 1500W appliance for long, so match your heaviest device against the watt rating and your runtime against the watt-hours before buying.
products.idealFor: Car camping, outages and van life where you need real wattage.
products.skipIf: You only charge phones and a laptop and want a lighter unit.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 Portable Power Station
products.verdict: 2 kWh in a body billed as the smallest and lightest at that size, with 0 to 80 percent in 66 minutes.
products.description:
The Explorer 2000 v2 is a high-capacity station billed as the smallest and lightest 2 kWh unit, charging from 0 to 80 percent in 66 minutes. Fast charging matters more than capacity during a multi-day outage, since a battery that takes eight hours to refill is hard to use between solar windows.

It ranks second because it doubles the capacity of the Explorer 1000 v2 for the $500-plus bracket, which is more than a typical weekend needs. Against the Explorer 2000 Plus it gives up expansion, but it is lighter and simpler.

Buy it for extended outages, work sites or off-grid cabins where two days of runtime matter. For lighter use the extra capacity is wasted weight, so check your daily watt-hour usage first and avoid buying more storage than you will ever cycle.
products.idealFor: Multi-day outages and cabins that need 2 kWh in a smaller body.
products.skipIf: You only need a weekend of camping power.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus Portable Power Station
products.verdict: A 2 kWh station that expands from 2 kWh up to 24 kWh and charges from sun or wall.
products.description:
The Explorer 2000 Plus starts at 2 kWh and expands up to 24 kWh with add-on batteries, and it charges directly from the sun or a wall outlet. Expansion changes the buying math: you can start with the base unit and add capacity later instead of buying a second station.

It ranks third because the Explorer 2000 v2 is lighter and lists a 66-minute charge, while the Plus leans on flexibility. Both sit at the $500-plus bracket, so choose the Plus only if you will actually add batteries.

Buy it if you are building toward a serious backup system or an off-grid setup. The expansion batteries are separate purchases and add significant cost and weight, so price the full 24 kWh configuration before assuming it fits your budget.
products.idealFor: Buyers planning a growing home backup or off-grid system.
products.skipIf: You want a simple one-box solution at a lower price.

products.name: Jackery HomePower 3600 Plus Portable Power Station
products.verdict: A home backup station billed as safe and plug-and-play, with few figures in the summary.
products.description:
The HomePower 3600 Plus is aimed at essential home backup, with safe power that lasts and a plug-and-play design. Plug-and-play is the useful promise for a household: you want something that works during an outage without wiring a transfer switch first.

It ranks fourth because the summary gives no watt-hour, charging speed or output figures, so you cannot verify the claims against the Explorer 1000 v2. It sits in the $500-plus bracket with the larger Explorers, and the home-backup positioning is the reason to pay for it.

Buy it if the goal is to keep a fridge, router and lights running at home. Read the full listing for capacity and output before you commit, since essential home backup means little without knowing how many watts and for how long.
products.idealFor: Households that want a station aimed squarely at outage backup.
products.skipIf: You want verifiable capacity and output figures up front.

products.name: Jackery Explorer 300 Portable Power Station, 292Wh
products.verdict: A 7.5 pound, 292Wh station that powers up to six devices.
products.description:
The Explorer 300 stores 292Wh, weighs 7.5 pounds and powers up to six devices at once. At that size it charges phones, tablets and a laptop several times over, and it is the only Jackery here that a single person can comfortably carry to a campsite or a tailgate.

It ranks last because 292Wh is a fraction of the Explorer 1000 v2's 1070Wh, so it cannot run a mini fridge or a heater for any meaningful time. It sits at $200 to $500, the same bracket as the 1000 v2, which makes the larger unit a better value unless weight is the priority.

Buy it for camping, travel and photography trips. Skip it for outages longer than a few hours, because its small battery will run out long before a fridge cycle completes.
products.idealFor: Camping, travel and photography trips with phones, cameras and laptops.
products.skipIf: You need to run a fridge or a heater.

whatMatters.detail: Watt-hours measure how much energy the battery stores, and watts measure how much it can deliver at once. A 1070Wh station with 1500W output can run a 1500W appliance for under an hour. Add up your devices' watts for the load, divide capacity by it for runtime, and check both figures in the listing before you buy.

Charge time decides how useful a station is across several days. The Explorer 2000 v2 lists 0 to 80 percent in 66 minutes, which means a wall outlet refills it in the time it takes to make dinner. Look for a stated time and a note on solar input, because slow charging stalls extended outages and wastes sunny hours.

Some stations accept extra battery packs, like the Explorer 2000 Plus, which expands from 2 kWh to 24 kWh. That lets you start small and grow, but the add-ons cost extra and increase weight. Check which battery models are compatible, and price the full configuration before committing, because a fully built system can cost several times the base unit.

Capacity brings weight. The Explorer 300 weighs 7.5 pounds, while larger units need a handle and often a cart. Decide how far you will carry the station, and check the listed weight. A heavy unit you never move is fine for home backup, but a burden for camping, so weigh the carry distance against the capacity you want.

Battery lifespan is measured in charge cycles, and the Explorer 1000 v2 lists a 10 year lifespan. Safety hardware such as temperature protection and surge protection matters for devices indoors. Search the listing for cycle counts and protections, and keep the station ventilated while it charges, since heat is what shortens a lithium battery's working life.

faq.q: Can a Jackery Explorer run a refrigerator?
faq.a: A fridge cycles on and off, so a station with enough watt-hours can run one. The Explorer 1000 v2 at 1070Wh can handle a fridge for part of a day, while the Explorer 300 at 292Wh will not last long.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with portable power stations?
faq.a: Buying on watt-hours and ignoring watts. The Explorer 1000 v2 lists 1500W, so it can start a coffee maker, but a heater above that rating will not run. Always check your heaviest device first.

faq.q: Is the Explorer 2000 v2 worth more than the Explorer 1000 v2?
faq.a: Only for multi-day needs. The Explorer 2000 v2 offers 2 kWh and a 66-minute charge at $500 and up, while the Explorer 1000 v2 gives 1070Wh at $200 to $500, which is enough for most weekends.

faq.q: How do I charge a Jackery station from the sun?
faq.a: Connect a compatible solar panel to the input port. The Explorer 2000 Plus lists direct solar charging. Check the panel wattage against the unit's input limit, and aim the panel at the sun for best results.

faq.q: How do I store a power station long term?
faq.a: Keep it in a cool, dry place at a partial charge and top it up every few months. Avoid freezing or hot garages, and keep the Explorer 300 and larger models away from damp floors.

faq.q: Can I take one on a plane?
faq.a: Airlines restrict large lithium batteries, so check your carrier's watt-hour rules before packing any Jackery. The 292Wh Explorer 300 is the smallest here, but even it may need approval, and larger units should not fly.

finalTake: Buy the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 if you want one station that handles camping, short outages and most appliances. Step up to the Explorer 2000 v2 for multi-day backup, or the 2000 Plus if you plan to grow the system. The Explorer 300 is the pocketable choice for trips. Match your heaviest device's watts to the output before you pay.
